opus-5.5.text:
Well, I wouldn't say it's completely meaningless, but I do think the way people talk about "AGI" today is not a well-posed problem. When you ask ten people what AGI means, you get ten different answers. Some say it's a system that can do every economically valuable task, some say it's human-level intelligence, some say it's something that surpasses humans in everything. If a term has no clear definition, no clear way to measure it, and no clear endpoint, then as a research goal it becomes more like a slogan, or even a kind of belief, than a scientific proposition.

The second reason is more personal, coming from my own research background in vision. I think a lot of the current AGI narrative is built on the assumption that if we just keep scaling language models, intelligence will emerge. Language is incredibly powerful, but it's a compressed, very human-centric description of the world. A lot of what we call intelligence, like understanding space, physics, causality, how to act in an environment, isn't really captured in text. A cat or a toddler has abilities that our best models still struggle with. So when people say "we're two years away from AGI," I feel that's measuring progress on a very narrow axis and calling it general.

And third, intelligence itself isn't one thing. It's not a single scalar you can push up until you cross a threshold called "AGI." Human intelligence is shaped by our bodies, our senses, our social environment, our evolutionary history. So the idea of one general intelligence that's universally better is a bit of a strange framing to me. I'd rather talk about concrete capabilities: can the system perceive the world, build a model of it, reason over it, and act in it? Those are questions we can actually do research on.

So for me, it's less about saying AGI will never happen, and more that I don't find it a useful compass. It tends to make people chase benchmarks and hype rather than the fundamental problems, and I think the fundamental problems, especially around perception and world understanding, are still wide open.

r002.rationale: It says language does not capture many kinds of intelligence, but makes no claim about human vision realizing a vanishingly small fraction of possible visual functions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I want to be careful here, because "false proposition" sounds stronger than what I actually mean. I'm not saying the goal is impossible or that we shouldn't be ambitious. What I'm saying is that AGI, as a term, isn't really a scientific proposition. You can't falsify it. Nobody can tell you what the experiment is that would prove we have it or don't have it.

Think about how we define it in practice. Every year the definition moves. First it was passing the Turing test, then it was "doing most economically valuable work," then it was "as good as a median human at any cognitive task." These are marketing definitions, or at best philosophical ones. They're set up so that whoever is speaking can declare victory or declare we're far away, depending on what they need that week.

And the "G" is the real problem for me. "General" implies intelligence is one scalar thing, that there's a single axis, and you climb it until you reach the top. I don't believe that. Human intelligence isn't general either. We're terrible at a lot of things. We're very good at a narrow band of things that mattered for our survival, and we got there through a very specific embodied, evolutionary path. So when people say "human-level general intelligence," they're combining two ideas that don't really fit together.

What I see in the actual research is much more interesting and much more specific. Language models got surprisingly good at language because text is a compressed record of human thought, and there's a lot of it. Vision is different. The physical world doesn't come with captions. Spatial reasoning, understanding how objects persist, how things move, what's behind something, these are capabilities where today's systems are still weak, and they won't fall out automatically from scaling text. So instead of asking "when do we get AGI," I'd rather ask concrete questions. Can this model build a world model from video? Can it reason about 3D space? Those are questions you can actually test.

There's also a cultural cost to the AGI framing. It turns research into a race with a finish line, and it encourages people to stop asking "why does this work" because they're too busy asking "are we there yet." A lot of the best work in the history of this field came from people being curious about a specific phenomenon, not from chasing a slogan.

So I'd put it this way. AGI is a useful story for raising money and recruiting people. It's not a useful scientific target. I'd rather we spend our energy on the actual problems, and if one day someone looks back and decides to call the sum of all that "AGI," fine. But that's a label you apply afterward, not a hypothesis you work toward.

astra-6.text:
I think the problem is that AGI sounds like a precise goal, but we haven’t agreed on what it actually means. What counts as “general”? Is it doing every task a human can do, doing most economically valuable tasks, or being able to learn something new? Those are very different claims.

Human intelligence isn’t a single threshold, either. People have different abilities, and we rely on tools, other people, and our environment. So imagining one moment when a machine crosses a line and becomes “general” may be the wrong way to frame progress.

That doesn’t mean I think AI has some fixed ceiling. Systems can keep becoming more capable and have enormous consequences. I’d just rather ask concrete questions: What can this system learn? Where does it fail? Can it operate reliably in unfamiliar situations? Those questions tell us more than debating whether we’ve reached AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d question the premise that intelligence has a single finish line. What exactly do we mean by “general”? General across which tasks, in which environments, and under what constraints? Without a clear definition, AGI can become a moving target: once a machine can do something, we stop treating that ability as evidence of intelligence and move the goalposts.

That doesn’t mean progress in AI is illusory, or that machines can’t develop much broader capabilities. It means I find concrete questions more useful: Can a system learn from limited experience? Can it transfer what it learns to an unfamiliar situation? Can it interact reliably with the physical world?

So my objection would be to treating AGI as a precise, binary destination. The capabilities are real research questions. Whether we eventually attach the label “AGI” to them is a separate question.
